                    ### Question
                    A 43-year-old man hospitalized for acute pancreatitis develops a high-grade fever and productive cough with gelatinous sputum. A sample of his expectorated sputum is obtained and fixed to a microscope slide using heat. A crystal violet dye is applied to the slide, followed by an iodine solution, acetone solution, and lastly, safranin dye. A photomicrograph of the result is shown. Which of the following cell components is responsible for the pink color seen on this stain?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Peptidoglycan
opb. Glycogen
opc. Protein
opd. Mycolic acid
ope. Capsular polysaccharide

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The sputum sample was stained using the Gram staining technique, which involves several steps: crystal violet dye stains all cells, iodine forms complexes with the dye, acetone decolorizes Gram-negative cells, and safranin dye stains the decolorized cells pink. The pink color indicates the presence of Gram-negative bacteria, which have an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharides. Peptidoglycan is present in all bacterial cell walls but does not contribute to the pink color in Gram-negative bacteria. Glycogen is not a component of bacterial cell walls and is not responsible for the pink color. Mycolic acid is characteristic of acid-fast bacteria and is not relevant here. Therefore, the pink color seen in the stain is primarily due to the presence of lipopolysaccharides in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, which aligns with the consensus on Gram staining. The most relevant option is capsular polysaccharide, which may be present but is not the primary reason for the pink color observed in this context.
